nodes.name: Shortleaf pine
nodes.desc: Pine dominates the south-facing slopes of the park. It tolerates fire and grows well on dry, nutrient-poor upland soils.

nodes.name: Blackjack oak
nodes.desc: An oak of dry ridges and slopes. Oaks and hickories dominate the cooler north-facing slopes, and their acorns feed many animals.

nodes.name: Sweetgum
nodes.desc: A common hardwood in the area whose leaves feed caterpillars and whose seeds are eaten by squirrels and birds.

nodes.name: American beauty-berry
nodes.desc: A shrub with bright purple berries that birds and mammals eat in autumn.

nodes.name: Virginia-creeper
nodes.desc: A woody vine of the forest floor and tree trunks. Deer, rabbits and birds eat its leaves and berries.

nodes.name: Luna Moth
nodes.desc: A large moth whose caterpillars feed on the leaves of trees such as sweetgum. It is often recorded around the park.

nodes.name: Eastern gray squirrel
nodes.desc: Eats acorns, nuts and seeds, and buries many of them, which helps spread oaks and hickories.

nodes.name: Eastern chipmunk
nodes.desc: A ground-dwelling rodent that gathers nuts and seeds. It is one of the most recorded mammals near the park.

nodes.name: Eastern cottontail
nodes.desc: Eats green plants and woody stems and is a staple prey of foxes, coyotes and hawks.

nodes.name: White-tailed deer
nodes.desc: The park's best recorded large mammal. It browses shrubs, vines and young growth and eats acorns.

nodes.name: American Robin
nodes.desc: Eats insects and worms and, in autumn and winter, many wild berries.

nodes.name: American Crow
nodes.desc: A very common omnivorous bird that eats eggs, small animals, carrion and fruit.

nodes.name: Turkey vulture
nodes.desc: A scavenger that finds carrion by smell and soars over the ridges of the park.

nodes.name: Virginia opossum
nodes.desc: An omnivore and scavenger that eats fruit, insects, small animals and carrion.

nodes.name: Raccoon
nodes.desc: An omnivore that eats fruit, nuts, small vertebrates and eggs. GloBI records many prey species.

nodes.name: Gray fox
nodes.desc: A woodland fox that eats small mammals, birds and fruit, and can climb trees.

nodes.name: Coyote
nodes.desc: Wikipedia lists the coyote among the park's mammals. It preys on deer, rabbits and rodents and also scavenges.

nodes.name: American black bear
nodes.desc: Hundreds of black bears live in the Ouachita Mountains. They eat mostly plant foods but also take deer and carrion.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Light on the forest canopy drives growth. Pine and oak dominate sunny ridges, shrubs and vines use the gaps.

nodes.name: Rain & spring recharge
nodes.desc: Rain soaking into the mountains feeds the hot springs and the forest, which is why the park is managed to protect the water system.

nodes.name: Wildland fire
nodes.desc: Shortleaf pine responds well to fire, which reduces competing trees and prepares soil for seedlings. Fire management is part of the park's work.

nodes.name: Thin rocky soil
nodes.desc: Dry, nutrient-poor upland soils suit shortleaf pine and post oak better than most other trees.

nodes.name: Fungi & decomposers
nodes.desc: Break down leaf litter, wood and carrion and return nutrients to the thin forest soil.
